Jot
JOT
noun
From the Greek iōta, the name of the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, answering to the Hebrew yodh — the least character in the Hebrew square script, a mere stroke no bigger than a comma; hence the smallest possible particle of writing, and so of anything.

Biblical Definition

A jot is the smallest letter there is — the Hebrew yodh, a single stroke hardly larger than an apostrophe, the least mark a scribe’s pen can set down. Our Lord chose it deliberately. Having declared, “Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil” (Mat 5:17), He measures the law’s permanence by its tiniest character: “Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled” (Mat 5:18). Luke keeps the same balance: “it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail” (Luk 16:17). Set the two halves of that scale side by side and the weight of it is staggering. On the one side, the whole created order — the mountains, the seas, the sun and the stars. On the other, one stroke of one letter of the Hebrew Bible. And the stars will go first. This is verbal plenary inspiration from the lips of Christ Himself: not the ideas of Scripture only, nor its themes, nor its general drift, but its very words, down to the least letter of the least word, are the breath of God and cannot fail. The psalmist had said it already: “For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven” (Psa 119:89). The Book is not a record of men’s reaching toward God; it is God’s speech, and He does not misspeak, and He does not lose a letter of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Greek iota, answering to the Hebrew yodh — the smallest letter of the alphabet; hence the least particle of anything.

expand to see more

JOT, the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, iota; the Hebrew yodh.

In the Hebrew square script the yodh is a single small stroke.

Hence, the least point or particle; the smallest imaginable quantity.

Not one jot shall pass from the law till all be fulfilled (Mat 5:18).

It is the measure Christ chose for the permanence of God’s written word.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:17 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."

Mat 5:18 — "For verily I say unto you, Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled."

Luk 16:17 — "And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail."

Psa 119:89 — "LAMED. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven."

Modern Corruption

The denial of inerrancy — the modernist and higher-critical dismantling of the text into sources, layers, and late accretions — is foreclosed by Christ’s own doctrine of the jot.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the denial of inerrancy, and it comes to us with a pedigree. Nineteenth-century German higher criticism, and its heirs down to the present, taught the church to hold the Bible at arm’s length: to carve the Torah into a documentary hypothesis of imagined sources, to invent a second and third Isaiah, to date what was early as though it were late, and to reclassify the Bible’s history as legendary material — and then to assure the faithful that the essence of Scripture survives untouched, since only the words are in question. Christ has foreclosed the whole enterprise. He did not say that the substance of the law abides, or its spirit, or its enduring principles. He said that not one jot — not one stroke of one letter — shall in no wise pass, till all be fulfilled. If the least letter cannot fail, the layers and the redactors and the late accretions have nowhere to stand.

Weigh the scale our Lord set up. Heaven and earth on one side; a single Hebrew yodh on the other; and Luke says it is the easier thing for heaven and earth to go. That is the dictionary’s doctrine of Scripture in one sentence from the mouth of the Son of God: verbal, plenary inspiration — every word, in all its parts, God-breathed, inerrant and infallible in the original autographs, and providentially preserved to His church. The consequence is practical and searching. If the words are God’s, then a man may not pick among them, nor keep the commands he finds congenial and lose the rest in the shuffle of scholarship; and Christ goes straight from the jot to the sixth and seventh commandments, driving them into the heart. He who would not let one letter fall will not let one commandment fall either. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven — and what is settled there is not open for revision here.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means the smallest letter of the alphabet — the Greek iota, the Hebrew yodh.

expand to see more

Jot — from the Greek iōta, the least letter of that alphabet.

It answers to the Hebrew yodh, a single small stroke of the pen.

Hence it denotes the least particle, the smallest imaginable part.

Christ measured the law’s permanence by it (Mat 5:18).

Heaven and earth shall pass before one jot of the word shall fail (Luk 16:17).

Usage

"One jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law — the stars will go first."

"Christ measures the word by its smallest letter: the very words are God-breathed, not the drift only."

"For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven — and what is settled there is not open for revision."
